claims.claim: Martin kills off central characters who are richly imagined, three-dimensional portraits, which most writers could not bear to lose.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters

claims.claim: Narrative momentum slows in books four and five, which become leisurely and expansive with overlapping, simultaneous storylines.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: the narrative momentum of the series has slowed

claims.claim: The appeal rests on the depth, texture and thoroughness of the imagined world and the range of imaginative sympathy across a large cast.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: depth and texture and profoundly satisfying thoroughness

claims.claim: The Bran defenestration lands harder in the book than on screen because Bran has already been established as a viewpoint character.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: even more of an impact, perhaps

claims.claim: Lanchester's 4,617-word essay contains no verdict on Martin's diction, sentence rhythm or dialogue; its praise is entirely structural (unpredictability, instability, the seasons as economic metaphor), and the LRB now serves the full text without a paywall.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013

claims.claim: Each chapter is narrated by a different character, so the reader's view of any character is partial, biased or wrong and must be revised as the tale evolves.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: each chapter is narrated by a different character

claims.claim: The fragmented viewpoint storytelling mirrors the theme of power fragmenting societies and individuals.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: This fragmentation in the storytelling nicely mirrors Martin’s larger theme

claims.claim: Martin replaces standard English with compound coinages such as 'sellsword' for mercenary and 'holdfast' for fort.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the compound coinages that replace standard English

claims.claim: The diction and the spellings of names are ingeniously quasi-medieval.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: ingeniously quasi-medieval diction and spellings of names

claims.claim: Period nouns (destriers, palfreys, vair, samite) give a strong sense of the concrete reality of the world and cannot be rendered on screen.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the perfumed language—the horses called destriers and palfreys

claims.claim: The narrative alternates distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus with exotic 'oriental' locales, bearing traces of Scott, Conan Doyle and Costain boys' adventure stories.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus alternating with exotic “oriental” locales

claims.claim: Tyrion's speech sets 'magnificent' destriers beside 'shit', a pointed mock-medieval deflation of romance that asks the reader to see beyond glitter to gore.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: The juxtaposition of “magnificent” and “shit” is pointed

claims.claim: The three-walled description of Qarth (animals, war, sex) reads as a sly reference to the series' own layered decor.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: a sly reference to the series itself

claims.claim: The view of court power is grimly unsentimental and Tacitean, with a tart Thucydidean appreciation of political corruption breeding narrative corruption.

claims.claim: Eastern cultures are rendered with Herodotean gusto (horse-worshipping Dothraki, quasi-Assyrian city-states, Venetian Braavos).
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: renders the Eastern cultures in particular with Herodotean gusto

verdicts.trueWording: the kind many writers couldn't bear to kill off
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'most writers' — the page says 'many writers', not most
verdicts.note: Quote 'richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters' is verbatim on the LRB page, in the paragraph listing Renly, Tywin, Robb and Joffrey ('He dies' x4), closing 'the kind many writers couldn't bear to kill off. Nobody needs to give Martin any advice about how he needs to slaughter his darlings.' The kill-off limb and the three-dimensional-portrait limb are fully supported; only the quantifier is inflated from 'many' to 'most'.

verdicts.trueWording: momentum slowed in books four and five; leisurely, expansive, overlapping
verdicts.note: Page: 'It's also the case that the narrative momentum of the series has slowed in books four and five, and the exploration of Westeros feels more leisurely and expansive, with the books' stories in many cases overlapping and simultaneous.' Every limb present; 'leisurely and expansive' is attached on the page to 'the exploration of Westeros', which the books enact.

verdicts.trueWording: depth, texture, thoroughness of the world plus imaginative sympathy
verdicts.note: Page: 'Add the depth and texture and profoundly satisfying thoroughness with which Martin has imagined this world, and the range of his imaginative sympathy with its large company of characters, and it's a wonder it's taken the world so long to fall in love with the books.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (world texture; sympathy across a large cast) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: equivalent impact in the books; even more of an impact, perhaps
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the flat comparative 'lands harder in the book than on screen' — Lanchester hedges ('equivalent impact ... even more of an impact, perhaps')
verdicts.note: Page: 'It has an equivalent impact in the books; even more of an impact, perhaps, because Bran has already been established as one of the characters from whose viewpoint the story is told.' The causal limb (already a viewpoint character) is verbatim-supported; the claim strips the source's hedge and asserts the comparison outright.

verdicts.trueWording: page prints '4617 words'; reasons named are structural; no paywall
verdicts.note: All four limbs checked against the full raw page fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200, complete article, no paywall interstitial or 'subscribe to read' marker anywhere in the HTML). (a) The byline block prints '4617 words'. (b) Read end to end, the essay contains no verdict on diction, sentence rhythm or dialogue: the strings prose, sentence, dialogue, diction, style, cliche and language do not occur in the article at all; Martin's dialogue is quoted ('grumkins and snarks', 'There are no men like me') but never appraised as writing. (c) The named reasons are structural and world-level — instability/unpredictability ('you genuinely don't know what's going to happen next ... That, I think, is the first reason'), magic as reader-only knowledge ('The second big reason'), and the seasons ('the second structural reason ... another economic metaphor ... Our freeze is economic, but still'); the remaining praise is for world-depth and imaginative sympathy, still not sentence-level. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM because the claim carries no quotation to match.

verdicts.trueWording: Rashomon-like: perspective often partial, biased or simply wrong
verdicts.note: Page: 'A striking feature of the novels is that each chapter is narrated by a different character. This device ... can have a Rashomon-like effect, since it often turns out that the perspective we have on a character or event is partial, or biased, or simply wrong. (One pleasure of reading the series is that you constantly have to revise your opinions and theories about the characters as the multiplex tale evolves.)' All limbs including the revision limb are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: power's use and abuse fragments societies and individuals
verdicts.note: Page: 'This fragmentation in the storytelling nicely mirrors Martin's larger theme: the way in which the appetite for, and the use and abuse of power, fragments societies and individuals; in a world ruled by might, who is "right"?' Quote verbatim, both limbs supported.

Page: 'Martin's imaginative linguistic evocations of his invented cultures: the compound coinages that replace standard English ("sellsword" for "mercenary," "holdfast" for "fort")'. Quote verbatim and both example pairs are the page's own.

verdicts.trueWording: the ingeniously quasi-medieval diction and spellings of names
verdicts.note: Page lists, among what a dramatization cannot render, 'the ingeniously quasi-medieval diction and spellings of names'. Quote verbatim; the claim adds nothing beyond it.

verdicts.trueWording: destriers, palfreys, vair, samite give concrete reality; undramatizable
verdicts.note: Page: 'Nor is there really a way to render, in a dramatization, Martin's imaginative linguistic evocations of his invented cultures: ... the perfumed language—the horses called destriers and palfreys, the gowns of vair and samite—that give you a strong sense of the concrete reality of this imagined world.' Both limbs (concrete reality; cannot be rendered on screen) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: bears traces of Ivanhoe, The White Company, The Black Rose
verdicts.note: Page: 'Martin's medieval narrative, the distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus alternating with exotic "oriental" locales, everywhere bears traces of the author's deep affection for the rather old-fashioned boys' adventure stories ... not least Walter Scott's crusader romance Ivanhoe, but also Arthur Conan Doyle's The White Company and Thomas B. Costain's The Black Rose'. All three authors named on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: mock-medieval epic asking us to see beyond glitter to gore
verdicts.note: Page quotes Tyrion ('those magnificent destriers shit everywhere') then: 'The juxtaposition of "magnificent" and "shit" is pointed: this is a mock-medieval epic that constantly asks us not to be fooled by romance, to see beyond the glitter to the gore, to the harsh reality that power leaves in its wake'. Every limb supported, and the speech is Tyrion's.

verdicts.trueWording: in the Qartheen decor a sly reference to the series itself
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the series' own layered decor' — Mendelsohn grounds the joke in the epic's 'slowly metastasizing' length (trilogy to five of a projected seven, each ~1,000 pages), not in any decor of the series
verdicts.note: The quoted Qarth passage does run animals (outer red sandstone), war (middle grey granite) and sex (innermost black marble), so the three-walled/animals-war-sex limb is exactly right, and 'a sly reference to the series itself' is verbatim. What the page does not say is that the referent is the series' decor; the tenor of the comparison there is scale — 'anyone familiar with Martin's slowly metastasizing epic—it began as a trilogy in 1996 and now runs to five volumes of a projected seven, each around a thousand pages long—will find it hard not to see in the Qartheen decor a sly reference to the series itself.'

verdicts.trueWording: Tacitean view of power at court; Thucydidean on corruption
verdicts.note: Two separate passages, both verbatim: 'One of the pleasures of Martin's series is the grimly unsentimental, rather Tacitean view it takes of the nature and uses of power at court', and, contrasting Martin with Tolkien's 'Christianizing sentimentality', 'he has, if anything, a tart Thucydidean appreciation for the way in which political corruption can breed narrative corruption, too.' Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Braavos is 'a cross between Switzerland and Venice'
verdicts.note: Page: 'Martin renders the Eastern cultures in particular with Herodotean gusto: the nomadic, Scythian-like, horse-worshiping Dothraki ...; the quasi-Assyrian city-states of Qarth, Astapur, and Meereen ...; the decadent port of Braavos, a cross between Switzerland and Venice, whose moneylenders finance the Westerosi wars'. All three examples are the page's own; 'Venetian Braavos' compresses a two-part simile whose other half is Switzerland, which does not unseat any limb.
